name: libblur
baseline: OpenCV imgproc (box_filter, gaussian_blur, median_blur; version not stated)
workload: Blur of a 3000x4000 RGB 8-bit image (also 2828x4242 RGBA and a 3000x4000 single plane), multithreaded, on a NEON machine and an x86 SSE/AVX machine: box blur radius 77, Gaussian kernel 151, stack blur radius 77, median radius 35.
claimed_speedup: Box blur 3000x4000 RGB radius 77: libblur 3.71 ms vs OpenCV 15.73 ms on NEON (4.2x, derived from page data) and 6.08 ms vs 43.59 ms on SSE (7.2x, derived from page data). Gaussian kernel 151, 3000x4000 RGB: libblur FixedPoint 26.68 ms and Exact 49.40 ms vs OpenCV 180.56 ms on NEON (6.8x and 3.7x, derived from page data); 30.72 ms and 43.41 ms vs 182.44 ms on AVX. Stack blur radius 77: 4.95 ms vs 8.43 ms on NEON. Median blur near parity (603.51 ms vs 637.83 ms on NEON). Single-thread box blur radius 15 on macOS: 11.46 ms vs Apple Accelerate 11.65 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README. rust-toolchain.toml pins nightly, Cargo rust-version 1.89.0, default features avx, sse, rdm, neon; the bench crate (app/Cargo.toml) enables sve, avx512, nightly_f16, nightly_fcma, fft and uses criterion 0.8.2 and the opencv crate 0.98.1 (system OpenCV, version and build not stated).
hardware: Not stated: README columns are labelled only NEON and SSE/AVX; the Apple Accelerate row says MacOS, so the NEON column is probably an Apple-silicon Mac. No CPU model for either column.
stars_or_usage: 88 stars; published as the libblur crate
tradeoffs: Rust crate (README says pure Rust; cbindgen.toml exists but a C API was not verified). Fast Gaussian and stack blur are approximations of a Gaussian and the README says they are not suitable for advanced analysis; FixedPoint Gaussian adds 1-3% error per README. u8, u16 and f32 paths; rayon threading; nightly Rust needed for avx512, f16, sve and fcma features.
caveats: README tables give no CPU model, OS, compiler flags, OpenCV version or OpenCV build, and do not say whether OpenCV ran its SIMD paths (standard OpenCV builds SIMD-optimise box and Gaussian filters, so probably yes, but unverified). Harness read in app/benches/box/main.rs and gauss/main.rs: (1) OpenCV calls allocate the output with Mat::default() inside the timed loop while libblur reuses a preallocated destination, which charges allocation and page faults to OpenCV only (material at 4-15 ms); (2) OpenCV box_filter is called with normalize=false (unnormalised sums, not an equivalent blur) and ksize 77 where libblur uses radius 77; (3) the OpenCV 'RGBA' box row reads IMREAD_COLOR (3 channels) while libblur processes 4 channels, which slightly favours OpenCV; (4) the libblur 'RGB box blur' bench feeds the RGBA bytes of test_image_4.png as 3-channel data and uses radius 35, while the README row says radius 77, and the Gaussian bench uses kernel 155 where the README says 151, so README tables cannot be regenerated exactly from HEAD; (5) Gaussian bench sets OpenCV threads to 1 then -1 and uses criterion sample_size(10). Fast gaussian and fast gaussian next rows have no OpenCV numbers. Same author as the listed sparkyuv and yuvutils-rs, whose harnesses had stride and label bugs. First-party numbers, partial methodology, so tier C.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/awxkee/libblur README plus app/benches/box/main.rs and app/benches/gauss/main.rs on raw.githubusercontent.com

name: FastGaussianBlur
baseline: separable true Gaussian blur (author's own implementation; no OpenCV or ImageMagick comparison)
workload: README graph of average execution time versus pixel count on a Ryzen 7 2700X comparing box-blur-pass variants of the repo against a 'true Gaussian blur'; README text gives one absolute figure for the template version.
claimed_speedup: No numeric speedup against a named library. README: 'blurs 2000k pixels in ~7ms on all cores of a Ryzen 7 2700X CPU with OpenMP'; the time graph is an image without numbers and shows a 'huge speedup' over true Gaussian blur.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile default target: g++ -O3 -fopenmp -std=c++17 (README does not say which compiler produced the timings)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++ template (fast_gaussian_blur_template.h), up to 4 channels and 10 box passes, border policies extend, mirror, crop and wrap. Approximation of a Gaussian: inaccurate near borders and for sigma <= 2 per README; modifies the input buffers; no SIMD (README notes an ISPC attempt did not beat it).
caveats: No comparison against OpenCV GaussianBlur or ImageMagick in the README, the ten issue titles scanned, or main.cpp (it only prints elapsed ms). README TODO lists 'redo timings'. The README figure is for the project's own approximation on an 8-core desktop CPU of 2018; no baseline row. An old issue reports slightly darker output with uchar arrays due to a non-rounded multiply (round_v added in v1.2). Lead for the orchestrator: the derivative michelerenzullo/FastBoxBlur (box blur only, based on this code) states in its own README about 2x-3x faster than cv::blur on an i7-10750H; that is a different project and not evidence for this one. Last commit 2024-08-18, so stale.

name: kornia-rs (Image.resize and imgproc kernels, kornia-py)
workload: Python bake-off on a 1080p RGB image, best-of-N minimum time per call with GC disabled (kornia-py/benchmarks/bake_off_pil_cv2.py and _bench.py): resize 1080p to 720p Lanczos, a resize matrix over bilinear, bicubic and lanczos for several shapes, and 13 image ops.
claimed_speedup: Resize 1080p->720p Lanczos: kornia 1.67 ms vs cv2 7.36 ms (4.4x) vs PIL 43.6 ms. Resize matrix (antialias=False vs OpenCV): 1080p->2160p bilinear 1.78 ms vs 9.80 ms (5.52x faster); 1080p->224x224 bilinear 0.25 ms vs 0.72 ms (2.84x); 1080p->540p bilinear 0.42 ms vs 0.82 ms (1.97x); 1080p->2160p bicubic 1.21x and lanczos 1.07x. Other ops: normalize 3.810 ms vs 67.76 ms (17.78x), ORB detect+compute 11.19 ms vs 45.51 ms. Score 9 wins, 4 ties, 0 losses over 13 ops; JPEG decode tied with OpenCV (39.64 ms vs 39.3 ms) and JPEG encode 0.94x.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.93.0, release build with opt-level=2 (LLVM bug workaround for faer), NEON intrinsics, rayon; pyo3 0.28, Python 3.10.12, numpy 2.2.6, OpenCV 4.13.0, Pillow 12.2.0, albumentations 2.0.8; run at commit 07e52d7 on branch feat/gray-f32-neon (2026-06-20)
hardware: NVIDIA Jetson Orin (aarch64), Cortex-A78AE, 6 cores at 1.728 GHz max, LPDDR5, JetPack R36.4.3, Linux 5.15.148-tegra
stars_or_usage: 720 stars; crates.io crate kornia and PyPI package kornia-rs
tradeoffs: Aarch64 NEON fast paths come first and AVX2 exists only for some ops; rayon multithreading; Rust crate plus PyO3 Python wheels and kornia-cpp bindings; antialias=True matches PIL semantics and antialias=False matches OpenCV INTER_CUBIC and LANCZOS4 semantics (different work). Pillow-SIMD is not in the matrix because it is x86-only.
caveats: First-party numbers, one ARM machine, no x86 results, measured on a feature-branch commit. The bake-off script calls k_img.resize(1280, 720) with default settings while cv2 uses INTER_LANCZOS4; the doc says kornia's 'u8 fast-AA path' beats OpenCV 'at the same kernel', but an antialiased kernel and OpenCV's fixed 8-tap kernel are not identical work (the aa=False matrix wins by smaller margins, 1.07x-3.09x). kornia uses rayon across 6 cores while OpenCV thread settings are not stated for resize rows (the grayscale row says cv2 6T). Page itself marks several 1080p ops below its 2x target and says resize 1080p is noise-bound (1.81-2.03x run to run). JPEG decode and encode are ties because all three use libjpeg-turbo. The page's own note says an earlier ORB-versus-VPI figure was inflated by harness overhead. The kornia-rs README has no benchmarks and Albumentations issue #1584 only states the claim without numbers. A WebSearch snippet of arXiv 2501.13131 (page blocked, snippet only) reports JPEG decode on Apple M4 Max of 1034 images/s for kornia-rs vs 1016 for OpenCV and 775 for Pillow; the current ternaus/imread_benchmark README no longer ships results or lists kornia-rs, so that independent figure could not be verified. Tier A rests on public harness plus stated Rust version, opt-level and CPU model.

name: go-gfx (resample package)
workload: Resize of a 1024x1024 RGBA image to 256x256 and of 256x256 to 1024x1024 with Bicubic, Lanczos and Box modes; go test -bench (ns/op) against Pillow best of 30 after warm-up on the same machine.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26.4, GOWORK=off, go test -bench; arm64 NEON axpy assembly kernel (resample/asmgen) plus multicore tiling; Pillow 12.2.0 with time.perf_counter
hardware: Apple Silicon (arm64), macOS, 16 logical CPUs; chip model not stated
stars_or_usage: 0 stars; 57 commits; README names go-images, go-widgets and go-webengine as consumers
tradeoffs: Pure Go with CGO disabled, float64 end-to-end (more memory and compute than 8-bit pipelines). SIMD assembly for amd64 SSE2, arm64 NEON and s390x; loong64, ppc64le and riscv64 use the scalar loop plus multicore tiling. Not bit-exact with Pillow: premultiplied-space PSNR 42.7-61.2 dB. Box mode is slower than Pillow.
caveats: Baseline is Pillow, not ImageMagick or stb_image_resize, and no golang.org/x/image or OpenCV comparison exists (the lead suggested one). The Go side uses multicore tiling across 16 logical CPUs while Pillow's resampler is single-threaded, so the ratio mixes algorithm and thread count; Pillow-SIMD was not tested. The Pillow harness script is not checked in (bench_test.go and perf.md only describe it), so the baseline side is not reproducible, and the chip model is missing, hence tier C. Repo is brand new (commits seen from 2026-08-28 to 2026-10-01, 0 stars). The vector package section only claims parity with earlier code, with no competitor comparison.

name: pic-scale
baseline: fast_image_resize (the baseline series of the repo's speedtest harness; no published result)
workload: No published result found. speedtest/src/runner.rs times RGBA8, u16 and f32 resizes of a 4928x3279 PNG, winter_huge.jpg and sample_fhd.jpg against fast_image_resize 6.0.0, pic-scale-safe 0.1.10 and Apple Accelerate and plots SVG charts.
claimed_speedup: none: no numbers on the README or any page opened
compiler_and_flags: speedtest crate: pic-scale features nightly_f16, rdm, nightly_i8mm, avx, sse; edition 2024; geometric mean of per-iteration times after 10 warm-up runs
tradeoffs: Rust crate with C bindings (picscale/), JS, Python and WASM bindings; runtime-dispatched NEON, SSE4.1, AVX2, AVX-512 and AVX-VNNI; nightly compiler needed for f16, i8mm and AVX-512 paths; 30+ resampling filters and colour-space-aware scaling (Lab, Luv, Oklab, linear, sigmoidal). README table says several paths (planes, SVE, some AVX-512) are only partly SIMD.
caveats: No speed number in the README, repo page, or search results; the speedtest harness writes charts and no checked-in results were found (speedtest folder shows src and Cargo.toml only). Harness bug found: in runner_rgba_fir the baseline destination is allocated with Image::new(target_size.width, target_size.width, ...), i.e. width x width instead of width x height, so for non-square targets fast_image_resize resizes to a different output size than pic-scale, which would skew any chart. pic-scale reuses scratch and destination buffers; fast_image_resize runs with default (single-thread) options. Same author as libblur, sparkyuv and yuvutils-rs.

name: scanx
baseline: golang.org/x/image/vector rasterizer via rasterx scanGV (GVScanner) and rasterx-family scanFT (FTScanner)
workload: Draw the whole SVG icon set in testdata/svg/landscapeIcons (parsed by oksvg, stroked by the rasterx Dasher) into an image.RGBA at 0.5x, 1x, 5x and 15x native resolution; ns/op per pass over the set (scanx_benchmark_test.go).
claimed_speedup: 5x: ImgSpanner 513,577,800 ns/op vs FTScanner 1,644,670,841 ns/op (3.2x, derived from page data) vs GVScanner 38,052,841,313 ns/op (74x, derived from page data); LinkListSpanner 227,859,937 ns/op (7.2x vs FTScanner, derived from page data). 1x: ImgSpanner 35,224,671 vs FTScanner 75,619,298 vs GVScanner 1,431,206,955. 0.5x: 14,352,161 vs 24,019,383 vs 362,814,157. 15x: ImgSpanner 4,173,881,468 vs FTScanner 10,811,718,931 vs GVScanner 250,690,083,743; LinkListSpanner 1,344,679,006.
compiler_and_flags: Go version and flags not stated; README prints goos linux, goarch amd64 and the -16 benchmark suffix (GOMAXPROCS 16); go test -bench
hardware: linux/amd64, 16 logical CPUs; CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 2 stars; default rasteriser of tdewolff/canvas (renderers/rasterizer imports scanx, go.mod lists it)
tradeoffs: README labels it beta with known bugs and recommends scanFT or scanGV unless each SVG is tested. LinkListSpanner has no gradients and can be slow on files with many random lines (rl.svg). Output differs from scanFT by up to 4 in a channel on randspot.svg. Meant for use with rasterx and image.RGBA or xgraphics.Image targets. Go only.
caveats: Baselines are Go scanners (scanFT and x/image/vector through scanGV), not Skia, Cairo or Blend2D, and there is no cross-language comparison. CPU model and Go version missing; at 5x and 15x most rows ran b.N of 1 to 5 times (single-shot). Times include oksvg path traversal and Dasher stroking. Per the rasterx README, ScannerGV draws through x/image/vector Draw with the path as an alpha mask; the harness gives it the full image bounds, which probably explains the 74x gap (not profiled), so the GV figure is not representative of x/image/vector on small paths. No LICENSE or COPYING file in the repo (raw LICENSE, LICENSE.md, LICENSE.txt and COPYING all return 404; the GitHub page shows no license), so the code is reference only. Last commit 2019-03-09.

name: plutovg
baseline: Cairo, Skia, Blend2D (category baselines; no comparison found)
workload: No speed comparison found. The README and repo page have no benchmark. The independent suite mfabbri77/VGCPU-Benchmark lists plutovg 0.0.4 beside Cairo 1.18.2, Skia m124, Blend2D, AGG, ThorVG, Qt and Vello CPU, but commits no result numbers.
stars_or_usage: 527 stars; rasteriser behind LunaSVG and PlutoSVG; v1.3.3 released 2026-05-18
tradeoffs: Small standalone C library built with Meson or CMake; path fill, stroke and dash, gradients, textures, text, clipping, compositing; single-thread software rendering. Sum-then-saturate coverage model (per VGCPU-Benchmark README), so self-overlapping subpaths inside one path composite differently from the exact-union model of Cairo and Skia. Rasteriser descends from FreeType ftgrays.
caveats: No speed number in the README, repo page, the 25 issue titles scanned (none about performance), the LunaSVG README, or two WebSearch queries. Lead: run mfabbri77/VGCPU-Benchmark (0 stars, MIT, perf/ holds only a scene list) to obtain tier A or B numbers against Cairo, Skia and Blend2D; its plutovg backend is version 0.0.4, older than the current v1.3.3. Usability marked mixed: project licence is MIT but the vendored rasteriser (source/plutovg-ft-raster.c) carries the FreeType Project License header (FTL, permissive with attribution, not OSI-approved).
